messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Thuan

Thuan was fifty-eight when the accident happened on a commercial roofing job in suburban Atlanta. He had been working in residential and commercial roofing for nearly thirty years—meticulous work that required precision and an almost meditative focus on the task at hand. That afternoon, he and a younger colleague were applying a sealant to the flat roof of a three-story office building. The product had been delivered in unmarked containers; the site supervisor assured them it was standard, approved, nothing to worry about. Within minutes of opening the first container, Thuan felt a burning sensation in his throat and sinuses. The smell was acrid, chemical, nothing like the familiar odors he had encountered across three decades in the trade. His colleague noticed it too, but by then both men were already inhaling the fumes. Thuan remembered the panic—the sudden awareness that something was profoundly wrong, that the air itself had become hostile. He stumbled toward the roof's edge, gasping, his vision blurring. Emergency services arrived within twenty minutes. The substance turned out to be an industrial-grade solvent that had been improperly labeled and stored; it contained compounds that caused acute chemical pneumonitis. Thuan spent four days in the hospital, where doctors confirmed that his lungs had been exposed to toxic levels of volatile organic compounds. He was discharged with a prescription for corticosteroids and an inhaler, told that his respiratory function would likely recover fully, though it might take months.

Eight years have passed since that day. Thuan is now sixty-six, and he has not returned to roofing. The physical recovery was complete—his pulmonary function tests normalized within a year—but something else did not heal. He came to believe that he could no longer trust his own judgment about safety, that he had failed to notice or prevent something catastrophic that nearly killed him. The world, in his mind, had become saturated with invisible dangers. What frightened him most was the thought that he might miss another warning sign, that the next threat could come from anywhere, disguised as something ordinary. He had come to believe he had no future worth planning for—that his body had been fundamentally compromised, that his capacity to work and contribute had been stolen from him.

When darkness falls, Thuan's vigilance intensifies. He lies awake beside his wife, Mei, listening to the house settle, unable to relax even in the safety of their bedroom. Waking in the dark triggers an immediate surge of dread; his heart accelerates, and his mind floods with the sensory memory of that afternoon—the burning in his throat, the chemical taste, the feeling of his lungs closing. The memory plays like a film he cannot stop: the moment he opened the container, the smell hitting him, the blur of panic, the ambulance. The images are vivid and intrusive, accompanied by the full emotional intensity of the original terror, sometimes arriving without any visual component at all, just a crushing wave of fear and suffocation. These nocturnal episodes have become so routine that Thuan now dreads bedtime. He tries hard not to think about what happened, pushing the memories away during the day, but at night his effort collapses. The suppression leaves him exhausted and hypervigilant by morning.

The smell of antiseptic—in hospitals, in some cleaning products, even in the waiting rooms of doctors' offices—transports him instantly back to those four hospital days and the chemical exposure that preceded them. When Mei needed a routine colonoscopy last year, Thuan accompanied her to the outpatient surgery center. The moment they entered the corridor and he caught the familiar sharp scent of disinfectant, his breathing became shallow, his concentration fractured. He could not focus on Mei's reassurances or the nurse's explanations. The threat felt immediate and inescapable. He sat in the waiting area gripping the armrest, unable to relax, certain that the air itself was contaminated. He left the building and waited in the car, avoiding the space entirely, unable to assess whether it was truly safe. This pattern has repeated itself: he avoids hospitals, avoids unfamiliar places where he cannot quickly identify exits or assess potential chemical hazards, avoids anything that might expose him to similar smells.

His avoidance has reshaped his life in ways both obvious and subtle. He stopped asserting himself with Mei, never disagreeing with her plans or expressing his own needs, believing that conflict might destabilize the fragile equilibrium he has constructed. He dwells constantly on how he used to be—the confident craftsman, the man who could read a roof and know exactly what it needed, the man who trusted himself. That version of him feels irretrievable. His inability to relax, his difficulty concentrating, his conviction that he cannot rely on himself—these thoughts reinforce his belief that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that he is powerless within it. Because he believes the world is dangerous and that he cannot trust his own judgment, he finds himself hypervigilant to any potential threat, scanning for smells, for darkness, for unfamiliar situations. This vigilance keeps him trapped in a state of perpetual threat detection, which in turn triggers the memories and the sense of helplessness that feeds his conviction that he has no future.

Mei finally insisted he see someone after she found him one morning at 3 a.m. sitting on the back porch in the dark, unable to return to bed, unable to explain why he was so afraid. She told him that he was disappearing, that the man she married was being consumed by something he could not name. It is this—the fear that he is becoming unrecognizable even to himself, that his life has shrunk to the size of a prison he has built from his own terror—that has finally brought Thuan to seek help.
